explanations.explanation: Jerusalem it is. The man says he's heading out to measure it, to find its width and length (Zechariah 2:2). He didn't say he was just wandering around with that measuring line. Somebody had a plan, baker.

I see why you'd go there, since temples are a very measurable kind of place. But the man says he's going “To measure Jerusalem…” and he wants its width and length. That's the whole city, not just one corner of it. The text names the city, so that's where the tape goes.

Judah sounds like a fair guess, friend, but that's a lot of ground for one man with one line. He says he's going to measure Jerusalem, its width and its length. A city, not a whole land. I'd still want a longer line than mine if somebody handed me the job.

That's it, baker. The message says Jerusalem will be a city without walls. The reason it gives is the multitude of men and livestock within it. So the man with the measuring line is heading out to measure a city that is going to have a lot of people and animals in it.

Double walls is a solid guess for a city that wants to be safe. But the message goes the other direction and says Jerusalem will be a city without walls. The reason it gives is the multitude of men and livestock within it. I'd have bet on walls too, baker, and I'd have lost that bet.

explanations.answer: A city high on a hill
explanations.explanation: A hill makes for a nice picture, but the message never says anything about height. It says Jerusalem will be a city without walls. The reason it gives is the multitude of men and livestock within it. So the news is about the people and livestock in the city, not about a view.

I can see how it sounds true, since walls and enemies go together in most people's heads. But the text gives a different reason. Jerusalem will be a city without walls because of the multitude of men and livestock within it. Nobody in this verse is tearing anything down.

False is right, baker. The message never mentions enemies knocking walls down. It says Jerusalem will be a city without walls because of the multitude of men and livestock within it. Then it adds that the LORD says, "For I will be a wall of fire around it…" (Zechariah 2:5).
Right. The LORD says, “For I will be a wall of fire around it, declares the LORD…” So the city has no walls, but it isn't left without protection. The LORD says He Himself will be the wall.

A tower of stone would be a sturdy plan, but that's not what the LORD says. He says He will be a wall of fire around Jerusalem. Notice who's doing the surrounding. The LORD says, “…I will be…”, so it isn't built by anybody's hands.

Angels do show up in this vision, baker, so I get the guess. But when the LORD speaks about the city, He says, “For I will be a wall of fire around it…” Not a ring of anybody else. He says He Himself will be the wall.
True. In the same breath as the wall of fire, the LORD says, “…and I will be the glory within it.” So He is around the city and inside it too. That's both ends covered, baker.

It's actually true. Right after saying He will be a wall of fire around Jerusalem, the LORD adds, “…and I will be the glory within it.” That's one verse holding two promises. Around it and within it, both from Him.

I get why you'd think so, since the verse mentions scattering. But the LORD says the opposite. He calls out, “Get up! Get up! Flee from the land of the north…” Nobody is told to stay put, friend. The LORD says it twice, so He means it.

False is right. The LORD says, “Get up! Get up! Flee from the land of the north…” and He says He scattered them like the four winds of heaven. That is a call to leave. Two "Get up!"s in a row is the kind of wake-up call I could have used back when I was stuck in the back of a junk drawer.

That's it. The LORD of Hosts says, “…for whoever touches you touches the apple of His eye…” The apple of the eye is something you guard with everything you have. So the text says anyone who touches His people has touched something He guards closely.

The work of His hands sounds like a good one, baker, but it's not the phrase in this verse. The LORD of Hosts says whoever touches His people touches “…the apple of His eye…” That's the part of the eye you'd shield first. I know a thing or two about being protective of my stamping end.

A crown is a fancy guess, friend, but the verse picks something else. The LORD of Hosts says, “…for whoever touches you touches the apple of His eye…” It's the apple of His eye, not a crown. That's the phrase to hold onto, baker.

Right. The one speaking says, “I will surely wave My hand over them, so that they will become plunder for their own servants.” So the nations that plundered God's people become plunder themselves. And it's their own servants who take it.

explanations.answer: Their kings make peace with Zion
explanations.explanation: Peace is a hopeful guess, baker, but it's not what the verse says. The one speaking says He will wave His hand over those nations so that they become plunder for their own servants. Nothing here about kings and treaties. It's about the plunderers becoming plunder.

explanations.answer: Their armies are sent back home
explanations.explanation: Sending armies home would be tidy, friend, but the verse goes a different way. After the wave of His hand, those nations “…will become plunder for their own servants.” Not a march home. The nations that plundered are the ones plundered.

True. Verse 9 ends with the one speaking saying, “Then you will know that the LORD of Hosts has sent Me.” The nations that plundered will become plunder for their own servants. And then God's people will know who sent him.

It's actually true, baker. The one speaking says the nations will become plunder for their own servants. Then He adds, “Then you will know that the LORD of Hosts has sent Me.” So God's people will know who sent him.

explanations.answer: He is coming to dwell among them
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. The LORD says, “Shout for joy and be glad, O Daughter of Zion, for I am coming to dwell among you…” The joy comes from Him coming to live among them. Not from anything else in the neighborhood, baker.

explanations.answer: Their new walls are finally finished
explanations.explanation: Walls would be a natural thing to cheer about, but earlier in this passage the message says Jerusalem will be a city without walls (Zechariah 2:4). The reason for the shouting is in the verse itself. The LORD says, “…for I am coming to dwell among you…” So the joy is about Him arriving.

explanations.answer: Their enemies are begging for peace
explanations.explanation: That would make for a loud cheer, friend, but this verse doesn't mention it. The LORD gives the reason Himself: “…for I am coming to dwell among you…” The joy is about who is coming. Not a word about enemies begging.

People is right. The LORD says many nations will join themselves to Him on that day, “…and they will become My people.” Then He adds, “I will dwell among you…” Many nations, and they're His people, baker.

Rivals is an understandable guess after all that talk about nations, baker. But the LORD says the nations that join themselves to Him “…will become My people.” Join Him and become His people, that's what the verse says. Rivals isn't the word.

Captives fits the plunder talk, friend, but it's not the word in this verse. The LORD says the nations will join themselves to Him, and “…they will become My people.” Join and become His people, that's the verse. People is the word.

True. The passage ends with, “Be silent before the LORD, all people, for He has roused Himself from His holy dwelling.” All people are told to be silent. The reason comes right with it: He has roused Himself from His holy dwelling.

It's actually true, baker. The last verse says, “Be silent before the LORD, all people, for He has roused Himself from His holy dwelling.” All people get that call, and the reason comes right after it. He has roused Himself from His holy dwelling.
